newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Higher US f'cast boosts world grains outlook.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Higher US f'cast boosts world grains outlook.

text.p: Improved expectations for the maize crop in the United States, where 1997 output is set to be the second highest ever, have led to forecasts of bumper world coarse grains production and stocks.

In a report released on Thursday, the International Grains Council (IGC) raised its estimate for 1997 world coarse grains -- mainly maize -- output by six million tonnes to a record 903 million, after 892 million in 1996.
The increase was mainly due to a higher crop forecast in the United States, particularly for maize, where the overall estimate jumped by six million tonnes to 277.1 million.
U.S. coarse grains output reached 267.6 million in 1996, the IGC said.
Industry analysts said that if the IGC projection were realised, the United States would turn out its second highest crop ever after the 284.8 million tonnes in 1994.
Good weather conditions and increased sowings were mainly responsible for the improved outlook, they said.
"They (farmers) have gone for these coarse grain crops in a big way and hence you've got this increase. Much of that is due to weather effects," said one analyst, who preferred to remain anonymous.
"Generally the outlook is very good, sowing rates have caught up and it's gone ahead very rapidly."
The prospect of increased coarse grains supplies in the United States also prompted the IGC to raise its world stocks forecast by eight million tonnes to 121 million -- the highest since 1993.

Analysts cited the 1996 Federal Agriculture Improvement and Reform (FAIR) Act, which authorised billions of dollars in fixed payments to farmers over the next seven years, as encouraging more cereals sowings.
In its other grains estimates, the IGC slashed its figure for Chinese wheat imports by three million tonnes to four million, more in line with the 3.4 million forecast for 1996/97.

Industry sources noted that a good Chinese wheat crop had reduced the country's import demand. The IGC pegged Chinese wheat output two million tonnes higher at 112 million tonnes after an estimated 109 million in 1996.
"They have better production prospects -- last year it started this way. They have better estimates coming in all the time," said one.
Iran was expected to remain a major wheat importer in 1997/98, in fourth position in the world league table with an estimated 4.5 million tonnes.
